name: Lash growth serum (peptide)
lead: Peptide lash growth serums are over-the-counter cosmetic products applied to the lash line to make lashes look longer or fuller. Some brands use peptides instead of prostaglandin analogues, and a reference work links this to regulatory rules in Canada and California.[1]

The best-documented lash-growth product is bimatoprost (Latisse), a prescription prostaglandin analogue; its manufacturer reports visible growth within 16 weeks and up to about 25 percent more length.[1][2] The sources reviewed contain no published human trials of peptide serums.

paras: Lash length is largely genetic, with upper lashes typically about 3 to 10 mm (usually 7 to 8 mm), and follicle number is set before birth.[1] Growth conditioners and serums, often built on seed extracts, minerals and other chemicals, have become common over the past decade.[1] Latisse, approved in 2009, was the first drug to receive FDA approval for eyelash growth.[1]

Bimatoprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue originally approved for glaucoma in 2001; its lash use is a cosmetic indication.[2] Its reported adverse effects with cosmetic use include infection if single-use applicators are reused and darkening of the eyelid skin.[2] Some cosmetic serums avoid prostaglandins and use peptides instead.[1]
No studies found on peptide lash serums. The reviewed sources describe studies only of bimatoprost.

timeline.event: Bimatoprost approved in the US for glaucoma.[2]
Latisse becomes the first FDA-approved product for eyelash growth.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, users ask which lash serum to use and compare options such as Latisse, a water-based serum from The Ordinary, castor oil and rosemary oil.[3][4]

claims.claim: Latisse is the lash serum to use for thicker lashes
claims.believers: A reply in a thread about thickening lashes after a month of castor oil recommends Latisse by name.[3]
claims.experts: Latisse is the only FDA-approved lash-growth product named in the reference sources, with the manufacturer reporting up to about 25 percent more length.[1]

claims.claim: Topical minoxidil can be combined with a lash serum for faster results
claims.believers: A poster asks whether combining minoxidil and a lash serum speeds growth; a respondent says they are different products and that topical minoxidil on lashes is not recommended.[5]
claims.experts: No published studies in the reviewed sources examine minoxidil on eyelashes or combined with lash serums.

claims.claim: A water-based peptide serum works as well as an oil
claims.believers: One user who gets results from rosemary oil asks whether a water-based serum saturates lashes and works comparably.[4]
claims.experts: No published trials of peptide lash serums were found in the reviewed sources.

card.summary: Cosmetic peptide serums sold for fuller lashes; popular, but no trials of the peptide versions were found.
card.note: Distinct from prescription bimatoprost (Latisse), the approved product.

quick.overview:
Lash serums are cosmetic liquids brushed along the upper lash line. Some use peptides rather than the prostaglandin drug found in Latisse.

The sources reviewed include trial-level information only for bimatoprost. No published human studies of peptide serums were found.
quick.mechanism: Brands claim peptides condition or support lashes. Bimatoprost, by contrast, is a prostaglandin analogue; peptide products avoid it, reportedly in part due to regulation in Canada and California.
quick.risks: Peptide serums are sold as cosmetics. For bimatoprost, reported effects include infection from reused applicators and eyelid darkening.
